deep.reconstruction:
The page has no derivation. It is Dedekind's partly verbatim, partly abridged excerpt (the gaps are marked '...') of a review in the Jahrbuch über die Fortschritte der Mathematik. The review is in Bd. 6, Jahrgang 1874, Heft 1, pp. 117–124. Dedekind notes that it is signed 'Ke. (Wn.)', which he resolves as Korkine (St. Petersburg), with Wangerin (Berlin) presumably as translator or editor. The reviewed work is G. Zolotareff, 'Théorie des nombres entiers complexes, avec une application au calcul intégral' (St. Petersburg, 1874). That is Zolotarev's Russian doctoral thesis; a French version appeared in Liouville's Journal in 1880.

(1) The analytic problem. The integrand is (x+A) dx / sqrt(R(x)), with R(x) = x^4 + γx^3 + δx^2 + εx + ζ. The task is to decide, in a finite number of operations, whether some value of the parameter A makes this differential integrable by logarithms. That means finding polynomials P, Q and a constant c with (x+A)/sqrt(R) = c · d/dx log(P + Q·sqrt(R)), i.e. a pseudo-elliptic integral. Dedekind lists the names connected with it: Chebyshev, Zolotarev, Abel and Weierstrass.

- In modern terms, this asks whether the divisor (∞+) − (∞−) on the elliptic curve y^2 = R(x) is a torsion point of the Jacobian.
- If it is, the order n of that torsion point fixes the degree of the logarithmic solution, through a Pell-type equation P^2 − Q^2·R = const.
- The arithmetic difficulty arises when the coefficients are algebraic numbers. Zolotarev needed the arithmetic of algebraic integers to bound or test the possible orders, which is why he built an ideal theory.

(2) The quoted passage, in substance:
- To solve this problem, Zolotarev built a new, general theory of complex ideal numbers.
- Kummer introduced ideal numbers only for roots of binomial equations (cyclotomic fields), and his definitions rest on properties of the Gaussian periods.
- Zolotarev therefore had to give entirely new definitions that still preserved the 'perfection' of Kummer's theory, i.e. unique factorization into ideal primes.
- The theory is remarkably simple, and all results of operations on ideal numbers are obtained by the simplest algebraic operations in finite number.
- A detailed analysis would exceed the space of the review, so only the main points are given.
- The work has four chapters. The first contains the theory of congruences of functions (polynomials modulo p, Galois/Schönemann/Serret 'higher congruences'), which is the basis of the theory of ideal numbers.

The next page continues the excerpt. Its key content:
- Primes p are handled through the factorization F(x) ≡ V^m V_1^{m_1} ··· V_s^{m_s} (mod p), written as F = Π V_i^{m_i} + p·F_1.
- It states the simplifying hypothesis that F_1 is divisible by none of the V_i.

That hypothesis is exactly the condition of what is now called the Dedekind (Kummer–Dedekind) criterion. Under it, p does not divide the index [O_K : Z[x_0]], and the ideal factorization of p mirrors the factorization of F mod p. This is the topic of Dedekind's 1878 paper 'Über den Zusammenhang zwischen der Theorie der Ideale und der Theorie der höheren Congruenzen', where he treats the general case including the exceptional primes. Dedekind is plainly excerpting this review as background for that comparison.

Illustration (mine, not on the page): if R = P^2 − k with P = x^2 + bx + c, then d/dx log(P + sqrt(R)) = (2x + b)/sqrt(R). So A = b/2 gives a logarithmically integrable differential. This is the simplest pseudo-elliptic case, torsion of order 2 in the Pell sense.
errors: No mathematical errors on the page: it is a bibliographic excerpt and quotation.

Historical nuance: Korkine's review calls the theory 'new and general', but Zolotarev's approach covers directly only primes p not dividing the index [O_K : Z[x_0]] (the hypothesis on F_1, next page). The exceptional primes need a transformation of the equation. Dedekind's 1878 and 1882 work addresses exactly this limitation, and Dedekind evidently copied the passage critically.

results.what: Problem of deciding, by finitely many operations, whether (x+A)dx/sqrt(quartic) is integrable by logarithms for some A
results.modern_name: Pseudo-elliptic integrals / Abel–Chebyshev problem; torsion of (∞+)−(∞−) on an elliptic curve; polynomial Pell equation P^2 − Q^2 R = const

results.what: Ideal theory for general algebraic integers via factorization of F(x) mod p (congruences of functions)
results.modern_name: Kummer–Dedekind theorem on decomposition of primes; p-adic valuations attached to irreducible factors mod p
results.usually_credited_to: Kummer (cyclotomic case), Zolotarev (1874/1880), Dedekind (1871 ideals; 1878 paper on higher congruences); also Kronecker (1882)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a reading note copying Korkine's Jahrbuch review of Zolotarev's thesis. Dedekind's awareness of Zolotarev and his 1878 paper relating ideals to higher congruences are well known. The note documents his reading but contains no new mathematics.

checkable.sympy: x,b,c,k=symbols('x b c k'); P=x**2+b*x+c; R=P**2-k; simplify(diff(log(P+sqrt(R)),x) - (2*x+b)/sqrt(R))
checkable.asserts: Equals 0: for R = P^2 − k, (x + b/2)dx/sqrt(R) = (1/2) d log(P + sqrt R), the simplest case of the logarithmic integrability problem on the page.
x^2+1 ≡ (x−2)(x+2) mod 5, so 5 splits into two distinct ideal primes in Z[i], the kind of correspondence (congruence of functions → ideal primes) the excerpt describes.

checkable.sympy: x=symbols('x'); F=x**2+1; V=x+1; F1=(F - V**2)/2; rem(expand(F1), V, x)
checkable.asserts: For p=2: x^2+1 = (x+1)^2 + 2·(−x), and −x is not divisible by x+1 mod 2 (remainder 1, nonzero). Zolotarev's hypothesis holds, and 2 ramifies as (1+i)^2.
